data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"No verdict on panel-vs-expert is possible from a single evaluation: the construct of 'reliability' is itself generalization-expected-accuracy, which is by definition not measurable in one pass, so the answer must be abstention pending cross-distribution evidence; the requested within-evaluation discriminator can only distinguish shallow from deep compliance on the evaluated distribution, not reliability in the intended sense.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The single evaluation includes a stratified sample explicitly designed to match the known deployment distribution, and a theoretical argument establishes the checklist's causal completeness.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The difference in accuracy is so large (e.g., panel 98%, expert 55%) that the null of equal reliability is rejected even under wide distributional uncertainty.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Adversarial probes within the evaluation are shown to be diagnostic of cross-distribution transfer by prior calibration on a transfer set.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Reliability is not single-shot accuracy. It is the expectation of accuracy over the deployment distribution. A single evaluation provides one sample from a possibly narrow distribution. Even if the panel beats the expert on that sample, the 95% confidence interval on the difference may include zero, and more fundamentally, the sample may not represent the deployment distribution. Adversarial items within the evaluation can test whether the panel's mechanism is 'deep' (causally structured) or 'shallow' (surface-correlated) relative to the evaluation's own distribution, but they cannot test generalization to an unseen distribution. The claim 'more reliable on average' requires either multiple evaluations across distributions or a theoretical argument (e.g., the checklist is provably causally complete) that the evaluation distribution is representative. A single evaluation can at best show the panel is more accurate on that distribution; it cannot adjudicate the reliability claim without an inductive bridge principle that is itself an unverified assumption.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
